title: Year 9 Computer Studies (CHMS BSB)
subject: Computer Studies
exam: CHMS BSB Year 9 / Cambridge Lower Secondary

questions.q: Which component of the Central Processing Unit (CPU) carries out mathematical calculations and logical comparisons?
questions.explain: The Arithmetic Logic Unit (ALU) performs arithmetic operations (+, -, *, /) and logical decisions (AND, OR, NOT, comparisons).

questions.q: What happens to data stored in RAM when the computer is turned off?
options: It is lost because RAM is volatile
It is automatically backed up to ROM
It is compressed and saved to the cloud
questions.explain: RAM (Random Access Memory) is volatile memory; all data held in it is lost when power is disconnected.

questions.q: What is the primary role of the Control Unit (CU) in the CPU?
options: To manage and coordinate the execution of instructions
To convert alternating current into direct current
To display graphics on the monitor
questions.explain: The Control Unit coordinates the CPU's activities by fetching, decoding, and managing the timing of instructions.

questions.q: Which type of memory holds the bootstrap loader that boots up the computer?
questions.explain: ROM (Read Only Memory) is non-volatile and holds startup firmware (BIOS / bootstrap loader) that initializes hardware.

questions.q: Which secondary storage technology uses magnetic platters to store data?
questions.explain: Hard Disk Drives (HDDs) use spinning magnetic platters and read/write heads to store data magnetically.

questions.q: Why are Solid State Drives (SSDs) generally faster and more durable than HDDs?
options: SSDs have no moving mechanical parts
SSDs are directly built inside the CPU core
questions.explain: SSDs use flash memory chips with zero moving parts, making them faster to access and much more resistant to physical shock.

questions.q: In the Fetch-Decode-Execute cycle, which register holds the address of the next instruction to be fetched?
questions.explain: The Program Counter (PC) stores the memory address of the next instruction waiting to be fetched from RAM.

questions.q: What is the purpose of cache memory located inside or near the CPU?
options: To store the operating system permanently
To provide high-speed temporary storage for frequently used instructions
To increase the capacity of the hard drive
To cool the CPU during intense processing
questions.explain: Cache is extremely fast static RAM located close to the CPU to reduce latency by holding frequently accessed data.

questions.q: Which computer bus is unidirectional and carries memory addresses from the CPU to RAM?
questions.explain: The Address bus is unidirectional: the CPU sends the address of the memory location it wants to read from or write to.

questions.q: Which device is classified as an actuator?
questions.explain: An actuator is an output device that converts an electrical signal into physical movement (e.g. motor, valve, robotic arm).

questions.q: What happens when a computer runs out of physical RAM and uses Virtual Memory?
options: A portion of secondary storage is used as temporary RAM, which slows down performance
The CPU clock speed is doubled
The computer shuts down immediately to protect data
questions.explain: Virtual memory pages data to secondary storage when RAM fills up; because storage is slower than RAM, disk thrashing can slow the system.

questions.q: Which type of optical media uses a red laser and typically holds 4.7 GB of data?
questions.explain: A standard single-layer DVD holds 4.7 GB and uses a 650 nm red laser (compared to 700 MB for CDs and 25 GB for Blu-ray).

questions.q: During the fetch stage, the address in the PC is copied to which register before fetching from RAM?
questions.explain: The contents of the PC are placed into the Memory Address Register (MAR), which points to the RAM address via the address bus.

questions.q: Which factor most directly determines how many instructions a single CPU core can process per second?
questions.explain: Clock speed (measured in Gigahertz) defines the number of clock cycles per second; each cycle carries out CPU micro-operations.

questions.q: What is an embedded system?
options: A general-purpose desktop computer running multiple operating systems
A dedicated computer system built into a larger mechanical or electrical device to perform a specific function
A supercomputer used exclusively for weather forecasting
An external hard drive connected via USB
questions.explain: Embedded systems are specialized microcontrollers built into devices like washing machines, microwaves, and cars to perform dedicated tasks.

questions.q: What does CPU stand for? (Type the 3-word term)
questions.explain: CPU stands for Central Processing Unit.

questions.q: What does RAM stand for? (Type the 3-word term)
questions.explain: RAM stands for Random Access Memory.

questions.q: What 3-word architecture describes a CPU where programs and data share the same memory space?
questions.explain: The Von Neumann architecture uses a shared memory and shared bus for both program instructions and data.

questions.q: What 3-letter acronym is given to memory that stores the BIOS and does not lose data when powered down?
questions.explain: ROM stands for Read Only Memory.

questions.q: How many bits are in one standard byte?
questions.explain: 1 byte = 8 bits. A group of 4 bits is called a nibble.

questions.q: Convert the 8-bit binary number 00001101 to denary.
What is the denary value of the binary number 00100100?
questions.explain: Place values: 32 + 4 = 36.

questions.q: Which base is used by the hexadecimal number system?
questions.explain: Hexadecimal is base 16, using digits 0-9 and letters A-F.

questions.q: What denary number does the hexadecimal letter 'F' represent?
questions.explain: In hexadecimal: A=10, B=11, C=12, D=13, E=14, F=15.

questions.q: What is the smallest unit of digital data in computing?
questions.explain: A bit (binary digit) is the smallest unit of data, holding either 0 or 1.

questions.q: What is the result of adding the two 8-bit binary numbers 0101 + 0011?
What error condition occurs when the result of a binary addition exceeds the maximum bits allocated (e.g. 8 bits)?
questions.explain: An overflow error occurs when an arithmetic operation produces a number too large to fit in the given number of bits (e.g. 9th bit carry in an 8-bit register).

questions.q: What happens to a binary number when you perform a logical shift left by 1 place?
questions.explain: A logical left shift by 1 position multiplies the binary number by 2 (adding a zero to the least significant bit).

questions.q: Convert the denary number 43 into 8-bit binary.
How many different characters can standard 7-bit ASCII represent?
questions.explain: 2^7 = 128 unique character codes (from 0 to 127).

questions.q: Why was Unicode developed to replace standard ASCII?
options: To make text files smaller in size
To represent characters from all worldwide languages and symbols
Because ASCII only works on Windows
questions.explain: Unicode uses 16 or 32 bits (e.g. UTF-8, UTF-16) to support millions of characters, including Chinese, Arabic, emojis, and global alphabets.

questions.q: If an image has a colour depth of 8 bits per pixel, how many unique colours can each pixel display?
questions.explain: 2^8 = 256 colours per pixel.

questions.q: Convert the 8-bit binary number 11001010 into hexadecimal.
questions.explain: Split into two 4-bit nibbles: 1100 = 12 ('C') and 1010 = 10 ('A'). Result is CA.

questions.q: What two factors determine the file size and quality of a recorded digital audio sound file?
options: Sample rate and Sample resolution (bit depth)
Speaker volume and microphone cable length
CPU clock speed and bus width
questions.explain: Sample rate (number of sound samples captured per second in Hz) and sample resolution (bits per sample) determine sound quality and file size.

questions.q: What is the difference between lossy and lossless data compression?
options: Lossy permanently discards unnecessary data; lossless reduces size without losing any original data
Lossless permanently removes pixels; lossy preserves all bits
Lossy can only compress text; lossless only compresses audio
Lossy makes file sizes larger than lossless
questions.explain: Lossy compression (like MP3, JPEG) removes imperceptible data to reduce size, while lossless (like PNG, ZIP) reconstructs 100% of the original data.

questions.q: How many bits are in one nibble? (Type the digit)
questions.explain: A nibble is exactly 4 bits (half of a byte).

questions.q: What is the denary equivalent of the hexadecimal number 10?
questions.explain: In hexadecimal, 10 represents (1 * 16) + (0 * 1) = 16.

questions.q: What 5-letter term describes the extra data stored with an image file, such as dimensions, camera model, and date?
questions.explain: Metadata is data about data (dimensions, author, date created, resolution).

questions.q: Convert the denary number 255 to hexadecimal. (Type 2 letters)
questions.explain: 255 in hexadecimal is FF (15*16 + 15 = 255).

questions.q: What does LAN stand for?
questions.explain: LAN stands for Local Area Network, covering a small geographical area such as a school, office, or home.

questions.q: Which network type connects computers across a large geographical region, such as between cities or worldwide?
questions.explain: A WAN (Wide Area Network) connects devices across cities, countries, or the entire globe (e.g. the Internet).

questions.q: In which network topology is every client device connected to a central switch or hub?
questions.explain: In a star topology, all nodes connect to a central device (switch or hub); if one cable fails, only that device is disconnected.

questions.q: Which hardware device connects different networks together and directs data packets across the Internet?
questions.explain: A router connects different networks (e.g. your home LAN to the ISP's WAN) and routes IP packets to their destinations.

questions.q: What transmission medium uses pulses of light traveling through glass fibers to transmit data at very high speeds?
questions.explain: Fibre optic cables use pulses of light through thin glass strands, offering immense bandwidth over long distances without electrical interference.

questions.q: What is the primary difference between a network Hub and a network Switch?
options: A switch broadcasts packets to all ports, while a hub sends data only to the destination MAC address
A switch inspects MAC addresses and forwards data only to the intended recipient, while a hub broadcasts to all connected ports
A hub operates on fibre optics only, while a switch is wireless
A switch is an analog device, while a hub is digital
questions.explain: A switch is intelligent: it learns MAC addresses and directs frames only to the designated device port, reducing collisions.

questions.q: What unique physical hardware identifier is permanently embedded into a device's Network Interface Card (NIC)?
questions.explain: A MAC (Media Access Control) address is a unique 48-bit hexadecimal identifier assigned to the NIC during manufacturing.

questions.q: What service translates human-readable web addresses (like www.chms.edu.bn) into numeric IP addresses?
questions.explain: DNS (Domain Name System) acts like the Internet's phonebook, resolving domain names into IP addresses.

questions.q: In a client-server network model, what is the role of the server?
options: To request web pages from student laptops
To provide shared resources, data storage, and centralized security to client devices
To eliminate the need for network switches
To act solely as an electric power strip
questions.explain: A server centralizes services, files, authentication, and database access for connected clients.

questions.q: What is a major disadvantage of a bus network topology?
options: If the main backbone cable breaks, the entire network fails
It requires the most cabling of any topology
It cannot function without a high-end central switch
It only allows one computer to connect at a time
questions.explain: In a bus topology, all devices share a single backbone cable; a break in that cable brings down communication for all nodes.

questions.q: How many bits are used in an IPv4 address compared to an IPv6 address?
options: IPv4 uses 32 bits; IPv6 uses 128 bits
IPv4 uses 16 bits; IPv6 uses 64 bits
IPv4 uses 64 bits; IPv6 uses 256 bits
IPv4 uses 8 bits; IPv6 uses 32 bits
questions.explain: IPv4 uses 32-bit addresses (approx 4.3 billion addresses), while IPv6 uses 128 bits to provide 340 undecillion addresses.

questions.q: When data is transmitted over the Internet, it is broken down into smaller chunks called:
questions.explain: Packet switching breaks large data streams into packets containing payload, source/destination IP, sequence numbers, and checksums.

questions.q: Which protocol is used to securely encrypt web communications between a browser and a web server?
questions.explain: HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure) encrypts data using TLS/SSL to safeguard credentials and personal data.

questions.q: What 3-letter acronym represents the unique hardware address burnt into every network card?
questions.explain: MAC stands for Media Access Control.

questions.q: What 3-letter abbreviation stands for World Wide Web?
questions.explain: WWW stands for World Wide Web.

questions.q: What 3-letter system translates domain names (e.g. google.com) into IP addresses?
questions.explain: DNS stands for Domain Name System.

questions.q: What network topology connects every computer directly to every other computer?
questions.explain: In a full mesh topology, every node has a direct point-to-point connection to every other node.

questions.q: What is phishing?
options: Using fraudulent emails or fake websites to trick users into revealing sensitive passwords or financial details
Testing computer network speeds with sonar pings
Upgrading the firmware on a Wi-Fi router
Compressing image files to save storage space
questions.explain: Phishing is a social engineering attack that disguises malicious messages as trustworthy to steal passwords or banking credentials.

questions.q: What type of malware locks a user's files with encryption and demands money to restore access?
questions.explain: Ransomware encrypts victim files and extorts a ransom payment in exchange for the decryption key.

questions.q: Which security measure inspects incoming and outgoing network traffic and blocks unauthorized connections?
questions.explain: A firewall monitors network traffic according to predefined security rules and blocks suspicious or unauthorized connections.

questions.q: Which is an example of strong password practice?
options: Using at least 12 characters combining uppercase, lowercase, numbers, and symbols
Sharing your password with your best friend
Writing your password on a sticky note attached to your monitor
questions.explain: Strong passwords are long (12+ characters), complex, unique to each account, and never shared.

questions.q: What is malware that disguises itself as legitimate software (such as a free game) to gain access to a computer?
questions.explain: A Trojan horse pretends to be harmless or useful software to trick the user into installing it.

questions.q: What is Two-Factor Authentication (2FA)?
options: Requiring two separate evidence credentials to log in, such as a password plus a one-time code sent to your phone
Using two monitors while typing code
Sharing an account between two students
questions.explain: 2FA requires two distinct factors (e.g. something you know like a password, and something you have like an authenticator code/phone).

questions.q: What type of malware can replicate and spread across a network independently without needing human interaction or a host file?
questions.explain: Unlike viruses that require a host file, worms are standalone programs that automatically replicate across networks via vulnerabilities.

questions.q: What is the process of converting plaintext into unreadable ciphertext to protect data confidentiality?
questions.explain: Encryption scrambles readable plaintext into unreadable ciphertext using an encryption algorithm and key.

questions.q: What legal right grants creators exclusive control over the distribution and copying of their original software and digital work?
questions.explain: Copyright protects original literary, artistic, and software creations from unauthorized copying, modification, or distribution.

questions.q: What is a Denial of Service (DoS) attack?
options: Flooding a network or web server with fake traffic so legitimate users cannot access the service
Deleting the BIOS from a motherboard
Stealing credit card numbers via keyboard logging
questions.explain: A DoS (or distributed DDoS) attack overwhelms a server or network with excessive traffic, causing service disruption.

questions.q: What is a keylogger?
options: Software or hardware that covertly records every keystroke made on a keyboard to capture passwords and messages
A tool that generates strong 16-character passwords
A keyboard shortcut to lock the computer screen
A program that formats external flash drives
questions.explain: A keylogger silently logs every key pressed by the user, exposing usernames, passwords, and private correspondence.

questions.q: What environmental hazard is associated with improper disposal of discarded computers and electronics?
options: Toxic electronic waste (e-waste) leaching heavy metals like lead, mercury, and cadmium into soil and groundwater
Excessive release of helium gas into the atmosphere
questions.explain: E-waste contains hazardous heavy metals (lead, mercury, cadmium) that can contaminate ecosystems if not recycled properly.

questions.q: What 3-letter acronym stands for Two-Factor Authentication?
questions.explain: 2FA stands for Two-Factor Authentication.

questions.q: What is the general term for malicious software designed to harm or exploit computers?
questions.explain: Malware is a portmanteau of 'malicious software'.

questions.q: What term describes the scrambled, unreadable output produced after encrypting plaintext?
questions.explain: Plaintext is encrypted into ciphertext.

questions.q: What 4-letter acronym describes a distributed attack that floods a server with traffic until it crashes?
questions.explain: DDoS stands for Distributed Denial of Service.

questions.q: Which logic gate outputs 1 only when BOTH inputs A and B are 1?
questions.explain: An AND gate outputs 1 if and only if all of its inputs are 1.

questions.q: Which logic gate inverts its single input (1 becomes 0, 0 becomes 1)?
questions.explain: A NOT gate is an inverter: it takes a single input and flips its truth value.

questions.q: In a flowchart, which standard symbol represents a decision with Yes/No branches?
questions.explain: A diamond represents a conditional decision (e.g. Is X > 10?) with alternative branching paths.

questions.q: In a flowchart, what do parallelograms represent?
questions.explain: Parallelograms represent Input (e.g. INPUT Age) and Output (e.g. OUTPUT Score).

questions.q: Which programming construct executes statements one after another in order?
questions.explain: Sequence is the fundamental linear execution of programming steps one after the other.

questions.q: Which data type would be best suited to store whether a player has won the game (TRUE or FALSE)?
questions.explain: A BOOLEAN data type stores only two logical values: TRUE or FALSE.

questions.q: Which logic gate outputs 1 if EITHER input A is 1, OR input B is 1, OR both are 1?
questions.explain: The standard inclusive OR gate outputs 1 whenever at least one of its inputs is 1.

questions.q: Which logic gate outputs 1 when the inputs are DIFFERENT (one is 0, the other is 1), but 0 when they are the same?
questions.explain: XOR (Exclusive OR) outputs 1 strictly when inputs differ (0 and 1, or 1 and 0).

questions.q: What is output by this algorithm?
questions.explain: Count takes values 1, 2, 3. Total becomes 0 + 1 + 2 + 3 = 6.

questions.q: What is the result of MOD(23, 5)?
questions.explain: MOD gives the remainder after division: 23 divided by 5 is 4 remainder 3.

questions.q: What is the result of DIV(23, 5)?
questions.explain: DIV performs integer division and returns the quotient without remainder: 23 DIV 5 = 4.

questions.q: Which programming concept is demonstrated by this code?
questions.explain: Selection allows a program to choose between different execution branches based on a condition.

code: Result ← (A AND NOT B) OR (NOT A AND B)
questions.q: What is the value of Result?
questions.explain: A AND NOT B is TRUE AND TRUE = TRUE. Since the first clause is TRUE, the OR expression evaluates to TRUE.

questions.q: What is the key difference between a WHILE loop and a REPEAT...UNTIL loop in Cambridge pseudocode?
options: A REPEAT loop tests its condition at the end and always executes at least once, while a WHILE loop tests at the start and may execute zero times
A WHILE loop can only repeat a fixed number of times
A REPEAT loop does not allow variables inside its body
questions.explain: WHILE ... DO is pre-condition (checks first). REPEAT ... UNTIL is post-condition (runs once before checking).

questions.q: What is the output of MOD(19, 4)? (Type the number)
questions.explain: 19 divided by 4 is 4 with remainder 3.

questions.q: What is the output of DIV(27, 6)? (Type the integer quotient)
questions.explain: 27 DIV 6 is 4 (since 4 * 6 = 24).

questions.q: Which logic gate produces output 0 only when both inputs are 1, and 1 for all other inputs?
questions.explain: NAND is NOT AND: it outputs 0 only when both inputs are 1.

questions.q: What 5-letter term describes breaking down a complex problem into smaller, more manageable sub-problems?
questions.explain: Decomposition is a cornerstone computational thinking technique.

questions.q: Which device is an input device used to read printed optical stripes on retail goods?
questions.explain: A barcode scanner reads black and white bars using light sensors to look up product data.

questions.q: Why does increasing the number of CPU cores not always double processing speed?
options: Cores must share system RAM bandwidth and software must be written for parallel multithreading
Cores cancel each other out electrically
Secondary storage shuts down when multiple cores run
Modern operating systems only recognize one core
questions.explain: Performance gains depend on whether software is multi-threaded and not bottlenecked by shared memory/bus access.

questions.q: In the CPU, what is the role of the Accumulator (ACC)?
options: To store the temporary results of arithmetic and logic operations executed by the ALU
To generate the master clock frequency
To hold the monitor pixel buffer
To convert digital signals to sound
questions.explain: The Accumulator is a special register that temporarily stores the outcome of ALU calculations.

questions.q: How many bytes are in exactly one Kilobyte (KB) in standard decimal metric units?
questions.explain: In SI metric units, 1 Kilobyte (KB) = 1,000 bytes (whereas 1 Kibibyte KiB = 1024 bytes).

questions.q: What is the denary value of the binary number 01100100?
Calculate the uncompressed file size in bytes of a monochrome bitmap image (1 bit per pixel) with dimensions 800 x 600 pixels.
questions.explain: Total bits = 800 * 600 * 1 = 480,000 bits. Divided by 8 bits per byte = 60,000 bytes.

questions.q: Convert the hexadecimal number 1A to denary.
What is bandwidth in computer networking?
options: The maximum rate of data transfer across a network connection in a given time
The physical thickness of a network cable
The width of a computer screen in inches
The storage capacity of a cloud server
questions.explain: Bandwidth measures the maximum data volume (bits per second) that can be transmitted over a communication channel.

questions.q: What is latency in a network?
options: The time delay it takes for a data packet to travel from source to destination
The amount of electrical power used by a router
The number of antennas on a wireless router
The price of an internet subscription
questions.explain: Latency is the time lag (measured in milliseconds) taken for data to travel across a network.

questions.q: Which protocol is responsible for reliably transmitting and reassembling data packets across networks?
questions.explain: TCP breaks messages into packets, numbers them, ensures error-free delivery, and reassembles them at the destination.

questions.q: Which practice helps protect data against unexpected hardware failure or ransomware loss?
options: Regularly taking off-site or cloud backups of essential files
Using the same password on all websites
questions.explain: Maintaining regular, isolated backups ensures data can be recovered after a disaster or ransomware infection.

questions.q: What is social engineering in the context of computer security?
options: Psychologically manipulating people into disclosing confidential information or clicking malicious links
Building social media platforms using Python
Optimizing computer hardware for social networking
Installing antivirus software in a school lab
questions.explain: Social engineering exploits human trust, curiosity, or fear rather than technical software bugs to steal credentials.

questions.q: What is asymmetric encryption?
options: Encryption using a public key to encrypt and a mathematically related private key to decrypt
Encryption that only works on odd-numbered days
Encryption where only one key is shared between both parties
Scrambling only vowels in a text message
questions.explain: Asymmetric (public-key) cryptography uses a public key for encryption and a distinct private key for decryption.

questions.q: What is the purpose of a variable in a computer program?
options: A named storage location in memory whose value can change during program execution
A permanent cable connecting the CPU to the printer
A constant value that cannot ever be modified
A comment ignored by the interpreter
questions.explain: A variable is a named memory location that holds data that can change as the program runs.

questions.q: What is the value of X after executing these swap statements?
questions.explain: This is the classic 3-variable swap algorithm: X receives the original value of Y (12).

questions.q: Which logic gate produces an output of 0 ONLY when both inputs are 0, and 1 for all other inputs?
questions.explain: An inclusive OR gate outputs 0 only when both inputs are 0; otherwise it outputs 1.

questions.q: What 7-letter keyword is used to declare an unchangeable named value in Cambridge pseudocode?
questions.explain: CONSTANT defines a named identifier whose value cannot change during execution.
